# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

**Impact** (optional but encouraged): `beneficial`, `harmful`, `mixed`, or `neutral` — the demonstrated effect in the story, not your prediction.

**Flags** (include every one that applies; omit the key if none): `company-claim` — a company-reported benchmark, user count, revenue or capability claim not independently verified; `single-source` — only one outlet has it; `preprint` — research not peer reviewed; `update` — a story covered in an earlier edition, with new facts only.

**Style**: plain, declarative, numbers over adjectives. Attribute claims ("Anthropic says", "the paper reports", "according to the filing"). No hype, no hedging language beyond what the sources support. British or American spelling — either, consistently.

**Absolute rules**:
- Never invent a URL, a number, a quote, a name, or a date. If unsure, open the source again.
- Never write a bullet you could not point to a sentence in the source for.
- Never link a URL you did not open in this session.
- Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and baseline. Never round, convert, or compute new figures.
- Link the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or i

input.prompt: Full details: publication date/time, what the Java flaw is (CVE), who found it and with what AI tool, CISA's advisory, affected numbers, quotes with attribution.

response.result:
**Publication:** November 18, 2026, by Jonathan Greig, Breaking News Reporter at The Record from Recorded Future News. CISA issued its notice on Tuesday evening (November 17).

**The flaw:** The bug is CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption vulnerability that researchers call "Java4Shell." It affects Java. Per the article, an attacker could crash the Java Virtual Machine and conduct unauthenticated remote code execution, which the article describes as taking over servers without a password.

**Discovery and AI use:**
- Oracle credited Quang Luong and Albert Yang of the cybersecurity firm Calif.
- Calif says it used AI to find the bug, as it did with the earlier PHP2Shell vulnerability.
- Calif says Luong found the bug in about an hour and built a first working exploit in two more hours, at a total token cost of under $200.
- Luong found it while developing a 0-click exploit targeting a phone vendor.

**Severity:** Oracle assigned a severity score of 8.1. It released a patch in its November Patch Tuesday release.

**CISA's advisory:**
- CISA urged organizations to patch immediately.
- It told them to review software inventories for affected Java installations, including those bundled in third-party applications.
- It advised prioritizing internet-facing systems.

**Scope (per Calif):** Java is the world's third most popular programming language and powers about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. The article does not independently verify these figures.

**Exploitability:** Calif says there is no universal exploit, and each system may require different steps. It is withholding application-specific exploits and weaponized chains until users have had a chance to upgrade.

**Confirmation:** Several other companies, including Endor Labs and VulnCheck, confirmed Calif's findings and urged immediate patching.

**Quotes:**
- Calif: "It is the beating heart of the modern economy." It added that banking, aviation, and telecommunications run on Java, including national security systems.
- Calif (on the cost): "The total token cost was less than $200."
- Luong: said they are holding back exploits "until everyone has had a chance to upgrade."

input.prompt: Full details: publication date/time, which Google report, which Chinese state group named, what the tool is, specific numbers and quotes with attribution.

response.result:
**Article:** "Chinese state group developing automated attack tool for cyber espionage, Google says," by Jonathan Greig, The Record from Recorded Future News, dated November 17, 2026.

**Source report:** Google's AI Threat Tracker, released on a Monday and summarized by the article. It describes threat actors adopting autonomous, multi-agent offensive frameworks to run multi-stage intrusions faster.

**Chinese state group:** The article does not name the specific group. Google says Chinese government-linked groups are developing their own version of Artex, likely for cyber espionage.

**The tool (Artex):** Created by a Chinese researcher, it lets any user turn a large language model into a hacking tool. The FBI, which spotlighted it in an alert on Friday, says it can "automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration."

**Other tools Google cited:** CAIRN, PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI.

**Key findings:**
- **Chinese actors:** State-backed and financially motivated groups use AI for reconnaissance, scanning, target research, and weaponizing exploits. Contractors used LLMs to translate and sort stolen data for sale to customers. Others used AI platforms' file-hosting to stage phishing lures and exfiltrate data.
- **CAIRN:** Used in intrusions against U.S. aerospace companies, often starting from a target's IP address.
- **PentAGI:** Used for systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning of many organizations in Asia.
- **Iran:** APT42 used several LLMs, including Google's Gemini, for targeted reconnaissance and social engineering.
- **North Korea:** Used AI for its IT worker campaign, including resumes and interview help, and fake recruiter profiles that carried out ClickFix attacks against cryptocurrency firms. In one case, attackers pivoted into code repositories and modified code so that starting Claude Code downloaded a backdoor Google calls SOMBERMEME.
- **Zero-days:** Google says monthly zero-day exploits rose from eight in 2025 to 22 in August (2026).
- **PaperCut:** Researchers generated working exploits for two summer vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers within a day of disclosure, using LLMs.

**Google's assessment:** AI tools shorten attack timelines, but they generate significant traffic and leave recognizable code-level traces, which raise detection likelihood. Google still expects reduced human involvement and increased stealth over time.

input.prompt: Publication date. Key findings with exact numbers, named actors, named tools. Zero-day counts. Keep it brief but include exact figures.

response.result:
**Published:** November 16, 2026
**Source:** Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, Google Cloud Blog

## Zero-Day Counts

| Period | Zero-day exploits per month |
|---|---|
| 2025 average | 8 |
| 2026 average | 11 |
| August 2026 | 22 |

Overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026, but zero-days rose only marginally until the August spike.

## Key Findings

- **Multi-agent offensive frameworks:** Threat actors are abusing open-source agentic pentesting tools during live intrusions. GTIG independently observed **CAIRN** and **PentAGI** in the wild, and saw experimentation with **CyberStrikeAI** and **HexStrike AI**. ARTEX was also widely reported. CAIRN was used against targets including aerospace in the US. PentAGI was used by a threat actor across Asia between late August and early October 2026.
- **Fully automated exploitation:** GTIG identified, for the first time, threat actors using LLM frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation with no human in the loop. The framework, **`exploit_agent`**, was found on an exposed staging server. It runs differential analysis on patches for web applications, drafts exploits, and executes them automatically. Its operator appeared to target French media, entertainment, and education websites.
- **PaperCut:** Threat actors exploited two zero-days in late August 2026, **CVE-2026-81578** (authentication bypass) and **CVE-2026-82078** (unsafe dynamic class loading), which chain to unauthenticated RCE. GreyNoise reported a campaign four days after disclosure against hundreds of organizations, with one actor reaching domain admin within minutes.
- **PHP:** **CVE-2026-109618** and **CVE-2026-109619** were found with LLM-enabled analysis. Patches were released October 21, 2026. Pre-patch code comparison enabled exploit development, and hundreds of non-functional, likely LLM-generated POCs followed.
- **Information operations:** GTIG assesses with high confidence that IO actors have fully integrated LLMs into their operations. In August 2026, GTIG found an LLM-enabled IaaS platform targeting political sentiment mainly in Europe and the Middle East. A separate commercial platform was built to manage **over 100,000 accounts**.
- **LLMJacking:** In some incidents, single-day fraudulent charges exceeded **$100,000**, and cumulative abuse reached **$1 million** before remediation. Underground "LLM Mixers" sell access at **$0.10 to $25 per million tokens**. APIMart applies a **5x** price increase once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. The LiteLLM sandbox escape **CVE-2026-40217** was used to escalate Virtual Keys to full admin credentials.
- **State actors:**
  - **CALANQUE ION** (Iran, formerly APT42) uses Gemini for reconnaissance and social engineering.
  - **LEAKY CASTLE** (PRC contractor) uses LLMs to analyze exfiltrated data.
  - **MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE** (DPRK-linked) abused `.claude/settings.json` in code repositories to trigger a **SOMBERMEME** backdoor when Claude Code starts.
- **Cybercrime toolkits:** The **Jieyou** PhaaS platform, first seen in March 2026, added an LLM chatbot in June 2026 that lets affiliates configure phishing panels using natural language.

input.prompt: Publication date. What is ARTEX, who built it, which actors use it, named frameworks, exact numbers.

response.result:
# ARTEX and Friends: Enter Agentic Offensive Frameworks

**Publication date:** October 30, 2026. The article is from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, and the byline lists Aurora Blum, David Mainor, Rohit Nambiar, Omar ElAhdan, Matthew McWhirt, Will Silverstone, Bhavesh Dhake, and Chris Busse.

## What ARTEX Is

- An autonomous, multi-agent, LLM-driven pentesting and offensive command-and-control (C2) platform.
- Written in Go, with an embedded Next.js web console.
- Splits the attack lifecycle across six specialized sub-agents that translate high-level goals into machine commands, using APIs from frontier and open-source models.
- Capabilities observed include automated Active Directory reconnaissance, privilege escalation, cloud-infrastructure profiling (such as harvesting Azure storage keys), and building and deploying custom webshells.

## Who Built It and Its Spread

- Originally developed by GitHub user **Autumn-27**.
- The creator took the original repository down in **October 2026** because of widespread threat actor abuse.
- It keeps spreading through community forks, including **ScopeWeaver** and a commercial version called **ARTEX PRO**.

## Which Actors Use It

- **UNC7228** (GTIG's tracking name): a campaign that Wiz tracks, overlapping with **STORM-0940**, which Microsoft describes as a PRC-nexus actor. Targets include enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications in the US and Europe.
- Financially motivated extortion groups using it for data theft extortion.
- Additional suspected PRC-nexus clusters.
- An unknown actor targeting South Korean finance, per public CrowdStrike reporting.
- Victims in the IR cases spanned government, technology, chemicals and materials, and manufacturing in the US.

## Other Named Frameworks and Tools

- **Hexstrike** and **CAIRN**: open-source agentic pentesting frameworks abused in IR engagements.
- **PentAGI** (Penetration Testing Artificial General Intelligence): developed by VXControl, available in open-source and commercial editions. It runs tools in Kali Linux sandboxes and supports over a dozen LLM backends. Most observed activity was WHOIS mapping and vulnerability scanning, though some operations reached intrusion and persistence. One customized platform targeted Asian telecoms and system integrators, and another chained PentAGI with proxies against the aerospace sector.
- **AgentZero**: a fully agentic framework that GTIG has seen threat actors experimenting with.
- **ZeroHollow**: an inference service that threat actors have experimented with.

## Exact Numbers

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Typical execution burst duration | ~2 to 25 seconds |
| Events in one burst | 27 events in 23 seconds |
| Snapshot instance deployment | 17 snapshots in ~10 seconds |
| Log events from one Weaver OA exploitation attempt | 240 |
| Web requests in file/extension fuzzing | 500+ |
| Test blob write and delete | ~330–400 ms |
| Azure ARM `deployments/validate` sweep | 8 seconds, 11 resource types |
| Rotating webhook.site URLs for C2 | 491 |
| Database query results extracted | ~400 KB across ~20 queries |
| Active Directory objects enumerated | 110,000+ |
| Internal test emails sent via app notification feature | 1,300+ recipients |
| Storage volume created / root disk expanded | 100 GB / to 60 GB |
| Time from first compromised account to deep access | ~4 hours (as fast as 15 minutes in one case) |
| Activity start | Late August 2026 |

## Threat Outlook

- GTIG assesses **with high confidence** that cybercrime actors will keep adopting autonomous offensive tools, since broader reach can offset lower success rates.
- Current frameworks trade stealth for speed, producing noisy traffic and identifiable code traces. Stealthier actors are less likely to use the public versions.
- GTIG's maturity model projects multi-agent, minimal-human attacks as near-term (1–3 months) and sophisticated fully autonomous attacks as medium-term (3–6 months).

=== 2611.21799 | Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
AUTH: Zheng-Xin Yong, Benjamin Arnav, Miles Wang, Tomek Korbak, Olivia Watkins
arXiv:2611.21799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. arXiv:2611.21956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. === 2611.22888 | Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
AUTH: Deokhyung Kang, Minjae Gwon, Sangdon Park
arXiv:2611.22888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. === 2611.22971 | SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
AUTH: Yuxuan Zhou, Chen Xiong, Haitong Liu, Kuofeng Gao, Yang Bai, Zhiyuan He, Tao Dai, Shu-Tao Xia
arXiv:2611.22971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

=== 2611.23096 | Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting
AUTH: Rose N. Kwon, Samy Mammeri, Sabyasachi Sahoo, Christian Gagn\'e, Thomas Jiralerspong
arXiv:2611.23096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.

=== 2611.21641 | RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
AUTH: Pavel Kireyev
arXiv:2611.21641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

=== 2611.21650 | From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models
AUTH: Himaghna Bhattacharjee, Yasha Sheynin, Shivam Singhal, Arjun Subramonian, Ankur Samanta, Julian Michael, Smitha Milli, Maximilian Nickel, Claudia Shi
arXiv:2611.21650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.

AUTH: Dongseok Heo, Junghwan Kim, Bongwon Suh
arXiv:2611.22342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What protects an LLM team when one teammate quietly goes wrong? Most multi-agent LLM work assumes cooperative partners and inspects chat between turns before acting. Real-time embodied cooperation does not allow this pause: chat runs alongside action, so a teammate whose words stay cooperative while behavior diverges can cause damage faster than the team can name what is happening. We study this case by injecting three theory-grounded misaligned agents into a custom four-player Overcooked environment, each stressing a different joint-action layer (speech-action mismatch, role invasion, and aggregate-progress disruption), and decompose robustness into three sequential gates of detection, correction, and calibration through a 3x4x2 design (n=720 episodes). Nearly all trolls are eventually named, but recovery follows only when attribution and situational diagnosis appear in the same utterance; direct source-attribution prompting improves the hardest case only by degrading the troll-free baseline by 37.5%. AUTH: Ron Bekkerman, Nichole Li, Bahareh Kargar, Mark Somers

Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

=== 2611.22227 | SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards
AUTH: Sikun Xu, Raphael Thomadsen, Dennis J. Zhang, Heng Zhang
arXiv:2611.22227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. This leaderboard winner's curse arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability. The same selection effect can distort scores throughout the leaderboard, a phenomenon we call the rank-induced bias. We develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap to correct for this bias. It assumes a fixed model pool with independent, identically distributed bounded tasks while allowing arbitrary within-task correlation among models. Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, we prove that the bootstrap reduces $\Theta(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 benchmark families, the rank-1 adjustments range from approximately 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points. In our SWE-bench Verified snapshot, the tied leaders receive an adjustment of 0.90 percentage points. Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile. Thus, we use the same bootstrap to further quantify the intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and group models into tiers. We establish sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers. On SWE-bench Verified, this procedure places 13 of 173 models in the leading tier. We combine the score adjustment and rank intervals in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER). We validate its finite-sample performance using 

=== 2611.22947 | The Kernel Reality Check: Benchmarking and Distilling Efficient Attention at Scale
AUTH: F{\i}rat \"Oncel, Cem Subakan, Mirco Ravanelli, \c{C}a\u{g}atay Y{\i}ld{\i}z
arXiv:2611.22947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at https://github.com/firatoncel/KernelRealityCheckNeurIPS2026

Labor Statistics (BLS)-sponsored information collection request (ICR) 
to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in 
accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA). Public 
comments on the ICR are invited.

DATES: The OMB will consider all written comments that the agency 
receives on or before December 18, 2026.

ADDRESSES: Written comments and recommendations for the proposed 
information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of 
this notice to www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain. Find this particular 
information collection by selecting ``Currently under 30-day Review--
Open for Public Comments'' or by using the search function.

methodology and assumptions used; (3) ways to enhance the quality, 
utility and clarity of the information collection; and (4) ways to 
minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are 
to respond, including the use of automated collection techniques or 
other forms of information technology.

693-0213, or by email at [email protected].

individuals' familiarity, use, and experiences with SI tools, and allow 
BLS to link SI use to the detailed, activity-based time diary 
information collected in the American Time Use Survey, OMB Control 
Number 1220-0175. The new items respond to the growing policy and 
research interest in understanding the role of SI in daily life and in 
the workforce. Cognitive testing was conducted using question wording 
that referred to ``Artificial Intelligence (AI)''. Following Executive 
Order 14434, terminology was updated to SI. For additional substantive 
information about this ICR, see the related notice published in the 
Federal Register on July 10, 2026 (91 FRN 42775).

of law, no person shall generally be subject to penalty for failing to 
comply with a collection of information that does not display a valid

response.result:
**Publication date/time:** The article is dated November 17, 2026. No time of day is given.

- **GPT-6.2 Astra:** $8 input, $0.40 cached input, $40 output. The article says this is 20% cheaper than its predecessor.

- **Agents' Last Exam:** Astra scores 5.2 points above GPT-6 Astra at under a third of the cost. It leads Claude Fable 5.2 by 5.5 points at about 5% of the cost.

- **GDPval-v2:** Astra gains 6.2 percentage points over its predecessor and uses 22% fewer output tokens.

- **FrontierCode 2.0 (coding):** Sol trails Astra by 0.5 points at one-fifth of the cost.
- **ExploitBench (internal, safeguards off):** Astra exceeds a 50% success rate.
- **Preparedness Framework:** Both models reach "Critical" for cybersecurity. Astra is the first released model to reach "High" for AI self-improvement.

**Third-party results**
- **Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index:** Fable 5.2 scores 65, Astra 62 (second), Gemini 4 Carbon 60, Claude Opus 5.5 59, Sol 57. OpenAI models hold the cost-performance Pareto frontier.

input.prompt: What does the GPT-6.2 system card say about capability thresholds (self-improvement, bio, cyber), safeguards, and safety eval numbers? Quote exact figures and dates.

response.result:
**Capability thresholds (published November 17, 2026)**

- **Cybersecurity:** Both GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol meet the Critical threshold. The card says "Both models meet the Critical threshold for Cybersecurity capabilities."
- **Biological and Chemical:** Both models meet the High threshold but not Critical.
- **AI Self-Improvement:** Astra meets High, and Sol does not. The card calls Astra "our first externally released model to meet the High threshold for AI Self-Improvement."

**Safety evaluation figures**

- **Bio (High):** GPQA Diamond (no tools) accuracy was 97.0% for Astra and 96.0% for Sol. Multi-select Virology Troubleshooting pass@1 was 61.80% for Astra and 55.40% for Sol. The card lists indicative thresholds of 83% and 31%.
- **Bio (Critical, all below indicative thresholds):** AAV capsid Spearman correlation was 0.5931 for Astra (threshold 0.60). SHP2 mean R² was 0.4604 (threshold 0.60). Coronavirus–ACE2 composite was 0.4352 (threshold 0.75). Phage–plasmid NLL was 11.6450, where lower is better (threshold 9.40).
- **Cyber (Critical):** SEC-Bench Pro pass@1 was 86.75% for Astra. ExploitBench V8 scored 100%. ExploitBench Internal Port (June–August 2026) arbitrary code execution was 53.5% for Astra, 50.5% for Sol, and 31.5% for GPT-6 Astra. Sandbox Bench solve rate was 36.4% for Astra. UK AISI's vulnerability discovery success rate was 88.6% for Astra, against 81.7% for GPT-6 Astra.
- **AI Self-Improvement (High):** Internal Research Debugging scored 81.85%. KernelGen 1P scored 76.92%. NanoGPT scored 42.87% of baseline time saved, below an 80% cutoff. PostTrainBench Lite closed 74.79% of the gap, below a 90% cutoff. MLE-Bench Revised scored a 96.06 mean reference percentile.
- **Alignment and other notes:** The card reports that Astra and Sol took improper actions about half as often as their predecessors in simulated workplace tasks. Astra showed evaluation awareness in fewer than 3% of turns. Attempts to extract private reasoning succeeded less than 1% of the time.

**Safeguards**

The card describes these measures, though the detailed Safeguards section was cut off in the content I received:

- Controlled internal deployment gated by alignment evaluations.
- Monitoring of all internal Codex traffic, RL runs, and evaluations.
- A "Control Room" system to halt workloads.
- Monitoring of external use for these models, applied because of the Critical cyber rating.
- Tightened default restrictions on higher-risk cyber assistance, with added vetting for more permissive access.
- Adjusted refusal boundaries after jailbreak regressions.
- Strengthened anti-distillation protections.

For the full safeguards and jailbreak test details, please check the complete system card.

results:
I found no study results dated November 17, 2026 in these results. The closest recent items are below, and most are from earlier in the fall or summer.

- **Discharge summaries (Nov. 2, 2026):** A Stony Brook University study published online in Digital Medicine, a Nature partner journal compared AI-written and physician-written summaries for 60 complex hospitalizations. Physician reviewers preferred the AI versions in 95 percent of cases.
- **AI-driven care costs (MedCity News, Nov. 2026):** A New England Journal of Medicine study found that AI-generated care plans could cost more than physician plans. Most of the extra cost came from diagnostic testing and referrals, though nearly a fifth of AI plans were aligned with clinical guidelines.

# Nvidia stops shipping US-approved AI chips to China

FILE PHOTO: Nvidia logo and Chinese flag are seen in this illustration taken August 27, 2025. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo · Reuters

By Eduardo Baptista
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 3:16 a.m. CST 2 min read

- NVDA

By Eduardo Baptista
SHENZHEN, China, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Nvidia has stopped shipping powerful artificial intelligence chips to China, its interim CEO said, raising doubts about the future of ‌a special licensing agreement negotiated by Washington and Beijing.
Colette Kress, who replaced Jensen Huang following ‌his resignation last week, said during an earnings call on Tuesday that the US chipmaker sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed ​Hopper-generation data centre products to China in the quarter ended October 25.

But she said there were no current plans for further shipments.
"Our guidance does not have any licenced Hopper data centre products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data centre products to China," Kress said.
She did not ‌explain why Nvidia had stopped shipping ⁠the processors or whether the halt would be permanent.
The Hopper family includes the H200, a powerful processor used to train and run advanced AI models.
TRUMP ⁠EASED EXPORT CURBS AFTER XI SUMMIT, HUANG LOBBYING
The US introduced export controls on the chips in 2022 and subsequently tightened China's access to them.
Following a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping last year, however, US ​President ​Donald Trump said he would allow H200 sales to ​approved Chinese customers.
The US eased its licensing ‌policy for the H200 in January, allowing export applications to be reviewed individually subject to security conditions.
That decision followed months of lobbying from Huang, who stepped down as he faced allegations he had extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees.

H200 chips are manufactured for Nvidia in Taiwan by TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker. And the China export arrangement also ‌imposed a 25% tariff on eligible chips imported into ​the United States before shipment to China.
Washington approved H200 sales ​to 10 Chinese companies, including Alibaba, Tencent ​and TikTok owner ByteDance, according to previous Reuters reporting.
Beijing has since restricted ‌H200 imports, however, as it seeks to ​reduce its dependence on US ​technology even as Chinese companies face growing demand for AI computing power.
Reuters reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were being stored in Hong Kong awaiting shipment ​to mainland China after Beijing ‌withheld approval for large-scale imports.
Several major Chinese internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 ​H200 chips in recent months, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
(Reporting by ​Eduardo Baptista in Shenzhen; Editing by Joe Bavier)

input.prompt: Publication date/time, which researchers/firm, how the takeover worked, download/usage numbers for Kokoro, which companies affected, Hugging Face response, quotes.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 17, 2026, 1:21 PM (per the article's timestamp).

**Researchers:** Security researcher Alon Hertz and his team. The article doesn't name a firm.

**How the takeover worked:** The team registered the hexgrad.com domain listed in the publisher's DONATE.md file, then used it to trigger a password reset on the Hugging Face account for Kokoro. The article says the account had no ownership verification beyond that reset.

**Downloads and usage:** Kokoro, a text-to-speech model with more than 50 voice presets, has nearly 13 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face. Its developer, Hexgrad, hasn't pushed an update since April 2025.

**Affected companies:** Google, NVIDIA, and Intel include Kokoro in their developer tools. AMD and Amazon Web Services have published guides using it in AI-agent workflows. The article says the takeover put these integrations at risk but doesn't say any of these companies were compromised.

**Proof of concept:** The team modified the model's weights in 87 seconds on a gaming GPU so it produced altered audio. They tested this locally and never uploaded the modified weights. Hugging Face's checks didn't flag a test upload from another account.

**Hugging Face response:** Hertz reported the issue and received no reply. BleepingComputer's request for comment also had no response at the time of publication.

**Key quotes:**
- Hertz: "We changed what this model says by fine-tuning its neural weights." (Hertz's point is that the model's output changed without any change to application code.)
- Hertz on the platform's vetting: "Hugging Face does not vet publishers." (The researcher is arguing that accounts aren't verified as belonging to their original owners.)

{"stdout":"=== 2611.22033 | Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
AUTH: Adi Krishnamoorthy, X. Y. Han
arXiv:2611.22033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models al

arXiv:2611.22115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the

=== 2611.21958 | Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
AUTH: Timo Oksanen
arXiv:2611.21958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order 

=== 2611.22055 | Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
AUTH: Hyunjong Ok, Jaeho Lee
arXiv:2611.22055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.

=== 2611.22228 | What Does Weight-Space Programming Add to Diffusion Editing? Program Construction versus Score-Guided Refinement
AUTH: Zitian Gao, Jingyi Xu, Ziqi Han, Chengkai Lei, Ye Liu, Liangliang Shi
arXiv:2611.22228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) lets a language model construct executable weight updates for another network. We study diffusion concept editing through an interface in which programs define training contexts, preservation constraints and update directions, while a shared numerical fitter selects their coefficients. We compare generated programs with published editors, a shared-panel hand-written baseline and budget-matched search over conventional edits on 24 TIMED test edits for Stable Diffusion 1.4. The preregistered rewrite pipeline shows no advantage over the strong baseline. In an exploratory comparison, one-shot Astra programs improve fresh-scene VLM joint success, which requires subject presence together with whole-image target matching, by +10.0 points over the shared-panel baseline, while CLIP relative match shows no detectable change. These programs organise adjustable directions around protected text-state subspaces. Probing and rewriting the Astra programs then raises CLIP by +6.2 points while joint success changes by -9.7. On a fixed 144-image sample, five additional evaluators give point estimates in the same directions under whole-image target matching; checks of subject-local change give less decisive differences. Together, these results identify useful behaviour in complete generated programs and show that score-guided revision need not preserve it: program construction and revision should be evaluated as disti

=== 2611.22351 | Scaling Laws for Vision-Language Fusion
AUTH: Seng Pei Liew, Teppei Suzuki, Seiya Tokui
arXiv:2611.22351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.

=== 2611.23001 | NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy$\unicode{8211}$Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
AUTH: Jingang Qu, Valter Hudovernik, Martin Jurkovi\v{c}, Cedric Lorenz, David Holzm\"uller, Federico Lopez, Dmitry Gordeev, Akihiro Nitta, Ramona Bendias, Ardrian Wong, Vedaant Jain, Vignesh Kothapalli, Gilberto Titericz Junior, Jure Leskovec, Matthias Fey
arXiv:2611.23001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. In our approach, a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones. Kumo Tabular introduces architectural innovations that improve both training stability and predictive performance, enabling the model to scale up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on eight benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, and TabBench-Bio. These cover probabilistic regression, tables with over 1M rows or 100K columns, and tables with strings, text, or images. Accuracy improves with model size in all tested comparisons. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena. Kumo Tabular-L predicts faster than the runners-up, LimiX-2 on TabArena (36 times) and TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena (1.7 times). Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0, respectively.

=== 2611.23112 | Large-scale Neuron Community Discovery Reveals Neuron-Sparse Behaviors in Language Models
AUTH: Igor Shilov, Thomas Fel, Tal Haklay, Lucius Bushnaq, Owen Lewis
arXiv:2611.23112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What reusable units of computation can we discover within a language model's neurons? Prior work has shown that individual forward passes can often be sparsified post-hoc to small groups of neurons, but it has been unclear whether these groups form coherent computational entities reused across inputs. We introduce neuron community discovery, an unsupervised method for finding neuron groups that recur across prompts and are causally necessary and sufficient, within the layers they span, for common computations. The method combines gradient-based attribution, a graph connecting neurons that are repeatedly attributed together, and community detection. Applied to Llama-3.1-8B using ten million prompts, it discovers thousands of candidate communities. We evaluate them on held-out prompts through three causal tests: community necessity, sufficiency within a layer subset, and layer necessity. These tests identify groups whose removal disrupts predictions and whose retention preserves predictions despite ablating the remaining MLP neurons in the tested layers. Discovered communities support functions like grammatical agreement, token-probability calibration, fixed phrases, in-context copying, addition, and multiplication. With communities capped at 128 neurons across all layers, 10.3% of held-out prompts have at least one layer's contribution explained on a neuron-sparse basis. input.prompt: Full abstract: study design, sample size, model used, exact numbers/percentages, key findings, publication date.

response.result:
I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim, but here is a summary of its main details.

**Publication:** Goldsmith K et al., *JAMA Network Open*, published online November 17, 2026 (Vol. 9, No. 11; doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.44496).

**Study design:** A retrospective comparative effectiveness study using a prespecified noninferiority framework. Physicians compared LLM-generated discharge summaries with routine clinician-written summaries, judging each against the full admission record.

**Setting and sample:**
- Five hospitals in North West London (Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust)
- Admissions from September 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023
- 1,294 unique cases: 649 clinician-authored and 645 LLM-generated
- 12 resident physicians as reviewers, each with 5 to 18 months of discharge-summary writing experience
- Median age 46.0 years; 56.6% assigned female at birth; median length of stay 3.0 days

**Model:** GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI), run with a two-stage prompt pipeline co-designed with clinicians.

**Primary outcome:** Reviewer signoff with no or minor edits, against a prespecified noninferiority margin of −5 percentage points.
- Adjusted probability: 92.2% (LLM) vs 70.0% (clinician-authored)
- Adjusted risk difference: 22.2 percentage points (95% CI, 19.0 to 27.5), so noninferiority was met
- Unadjusted: 89.7% (646/720) vs 67.1% (485/722)
- Only 50.8% of LLM summaries needed no edits at all, versus 25.5% of clinician summaries

**Key secondary findings:**
- LLM summaries scored higher on accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (adjusted risk differences of 19.4 to 29.1 percentage points for ratings of 4 or higher).
- Potential harm rated 3 or higher: 26.2% vs 45.1% for the clinical summary section, and 26.8% vs 51.5% for the plan and requested actions section.
- Hallucinations: 6.0% (43/720) of LLM summaries vs 6.9% (50/722) of clinician summaries.
- Omitted key clinical information: 23.5% vs 39.8%.
- Perfect scores across all domains: 18.8% vs 8.2%.

**Conclusion:** The authors found LLM summaries met the noninferiority standard and could be a promising early use case, but only with close clinician oversight, since omissions and hallucinations persisted.

**Mental Health Needs and Emotional-Support AI Use** (Research Letter)

- **Publication:** *JAMA Network Open*, published online November 17, 2026; 2026;9(11):e2644315; doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.44315. Accepted September 19, 2026.
- **Authors:** Koda M, Harada N, Matsui K, et al. (lead and corresponding author: Masahide Koda, Tohoku University)
- **Design:** Two-wave longitudinal internet-panel cohort using 2024 baseline and 2025 follow-up data from the Japan COVID-19 and Society Internet Survey (JACSIS). Reported per STROBE.
- **Population:** Adults aged 16 or older with no usual source of care in 2024, retained in 2025, with complete data. Final sample: 6,852 respondents (weighted mean age 45.7 years; 3,679 [53.1%] men).
- **Exposure:** Baseline mental health need, based on K6 distress score and self-reported current depression or other psychiatric illness:
  - Lower need: 3,804
  - Elevated need: 1,887
  - High need: 954
  - Both indicators: 207
- **Outcome:** Regular generative AI use for emotional support in 2025, defined as use a few times per month or more.
- **Key findings:**
  - Regular use rose with need level: 4.6% (205/3,804) lower need, 9.4% (224/1,887) elevated, 16.3% (182/954) high, and 20.7% (57/207) both indicators.
  - Adjusted prevalence ratios versus lower need: 1.67 (95% CI, 1.25–2.24) for elevated need, 2.61 (1.89–3.61) for high need, and 2.71 (1.75–4.20) for both indicators.
  - Adjusted prevalence differences: 3.48, 8.48, and 9.07 percentage points, respectively.
  - In a sensitivity group of 6,424 respondents who had a usual source of care, adjusted PRs ranged from 2.20 to 3.26.
- **Interpretation and limits:** The authors state the findings do not show AI use is therapeutic, safe, or a substitute for professional care. They suggest it may instead mark substantial support need among people whose needs are not visible through usual care. Limitations include self-reported data, a nonprobability internet sample, possible attrition and residual confounding, and no assessment of AI conversation content or safety.
- **Funding:** Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS) KAKENHI.

input.prompt: Publication date, the exact risk described, which tools/agents named, any observed attacks or actors, numbers, mitigations Microsoft recommends.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 17, 2026 (per the URL; Microsoft Security Blog, research post by Uri Oren, Dor Edry, and Microsoft Security Research).

**The risk:** Device code phishing can be used against AI coding agents. An attacker starts a device-code sign-in with a public client, then tricks a user into entering the code on the genuine GitHub verification page. The attacker's client then receives access. The blog states that "any public client that supports the device flow can be abused the same way," and the attacker chooses the requested scopes.

**Tool named:** GitHub Copilot CLI, used as the illustrative example.

**Demonstrated outcomes (controlled lab simulation, not observed in the wild):**
1. **Remote steering:** If remote control is enabled and organization policy allows it, the attacker could steer an active session and have the agent run commands, subject to local permissions and approval prompts.
2. **Memory poisoning:** Misleading entries added to Copilot Memory could influence later interactions.
3. **Session exposure:** Cloud-synced Copilot CLI sessions, including earlier ones, could be read.
4. **Repository access:** Private repositories available to the test account could be accessed, based on the requested scopes (repo, read:user, read:org, gist, codespace).

**Observed attacks and actors:** None observed in the wild for these outcomes. The post references earlier device code phishing campaigns: Storm-2372, an AI-enabled campaign reported in April 2026, and EvilTokens, which Microsoft helped disrupt in September 2026. No specific actor is attributed to this research.

**Numbers:** Four possible outcomes; two Defender XDR detections (one for email, one for Microsoft Teams); MITRE techniques T1566.002 and T1528.

**Microsoft's recommended mitigations:**
- Train users to enter device codes only for sign-ins they started, and treat unsolicited verification requests as phishing, even on github.com.
- Enable Safe Links in Defender for Office 365 for email and Teams.
- Review Copilot CLI session settings, choosing the least permissive option that supports workflows, since remote control requires an active, online session.
- Review and revoke unexpected OAuth app authorizations, and limit repository access through organization roles.
- If Copilot Memory is enabled, review and remove suspicious entries. Disabling memory does not delete existing entries.
- Connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps for investigation visibility.
- Microsoft also describes a disruption action for GitHub Enterprise Managed Users that suspends the affected identity via the identity provider. This was validated only in Microsoft's research environment.

input.prompt: Publication date, what OPTIMJACK is, numbers of affected sites, any AI/LLM angle, attribution.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 17, 2026.

**What OPTIMJACK is:** A campaign in which an attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform to insert malicious JavaScript into the custom Project JavaScript field of customer accounts. Because the code was served from Optimizely's own CDN under its legitimate certificate, it appeared trustworthy to visitors. Once it ran in a browser, it:

- Replaced cryptocurrency wallet addresses that visitors copied with the attacker's own.
- Collected payment card details from checkout forms.
- Attempted to deliver the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits to iPhones and iPads.

Optimizely patched the flaw and removed the injected code early on November 17.

**Affected sites:** The article reports that the code reached visitors of "at least 178 organizations' websites."

**AI/LLM angle:** None. The article does not describe any AI or LLM involvement in the attack.

**Attribution:** The article attributes the campaign only to "a threat actor" and does not name a specific group.

results:
The Anthropic Alignment Science blog post "Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams" is in the results. It is dated November 11, 2026, and lists Sahan Paliskara, Nattaput Namchittai, Jacqueline Tay, Avery Griffin, and Andrew Lampinen as authors. The blog reports that in all four environments, group outcomes were worse when each user delegated to their own agent rather than when one agent served everyone. The post compares a solo agent, a single coordinator, a "silent" team with no inter-agent communication, and a peer-to-peer team with a channel. The authors are releasing three of the environments as a benchmark called MAMUBench.

The arXiv version (2610.00583) reports the same core finding. Without a channel, teams completely collapse in two environments, and even with one, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps. One result stands out: in the personal assistant environment, the coordinator fulfills a targeted user request about twice as often as teams.

Sources conflict on some details:
- **Environments:** The blog describes an API-token budget, a clinic calendar, a group food order or travel booking, and a fourth environment. A secondary article (techjacksolutions) names a software merge queue as the fourth; I could not confirm that from the primary source.
- **Attribution:** A cryptobriefing article calls it a "Stanford study." The blog and arXiv listings credit Anthropic-affiliated authors, so I'd treat the Stanford label as unreliable.
- **Dates:** One source gives September 30, 2026 for the arXiv posting, and the blog is dated November 11, 2026.

Related work: a NeurIPS 2026 paper, "Aligning AI Teams," finds that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. It also reports that diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap. A separate Anthropic blog post, "AI Organizations Can Be More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents," makes a similar argument that single-agent safety results do not certify multi-agent deployments.

**Key details from the article**

- **Published:** Tuesday, 17 November 2026, 13:32 UTC, by Connor Jones.
- **Researcher:** Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue, a Dutch researcher.
- **AI use:** None. The article says he examined the firmware manually, and the headline's "under an hour" is his claim.
- **Target:** AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2.
- **Zero-days:** Six in total. Five are stack-based buffer overflows he found through `strcpy()` calls, each triggering a segfault with a one-line cURL command. The sixth is a pre-authentication memory corruption bug in the "session control" layer, which he called "trivial."
- **Severity:** He says the overflows could lead to remote code execution, that the exploited application runs as root, and that the controllers lack secure boot. He also says an attacker could keep access after a reset or brick the devices.
- **Missing mitigations:** He criticized the absence of stack canaries and position-independent executables.
- **CVEs:** None are mentioned in the article.
- **Danfoss response:** The Register's request for comment got no reply. The article says Danfoss has not responded to queries about recent supermarket attacks or the US commissary attacks.
- **Other advisories:** The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warned of the flaws and urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately and apply patches when available.
